title: Temple and family
hookLine: in much of Asia, ancestor offerings and temple festivals are part of Buddhist life

cards: A low shelf by the kitchen door. On it: a figure of the Buddha, a photograph of a grandmother, a bowl of oranges, a cup of tea just poured, a stick of incense still smoking.
A child is told to bow before breakfast, and does, half asleep.
In a home like this, that's what Buddhism looks like on a weekday: not a retreat or a lecture but a shelf where the family's living and dead are kept close together.

teach.b: First, the altar. In Japan it's often a butsudan, a Buddha cabinet with the family's memorial tablets. In Chinese and Vietnamese homes there may be an ancestor shelf beside the Buddha image.
Families offer food, flowers, light and incense, and they talk to their dead, telling them the news. Second, the old root.

A short Pali text, the Tirokudda Sutta, pictures the departed standing outside the walls and at the crossroads, waiting at the homes where they once lived. Weeping and grief, it says, don't help them.
What helps is giving in their name: food and gifts offered to the monks, the good of it dedicated to the dead.

And in the Sigalovada Sutta, the Buddha tells a young man that one way to honor his parents is to make offerings for them when they're gone. Third, the festivals, which day six eighty-six met as Obon.

Tradition tells of the monk Maudgalyayana, who saw his mother suffering after death and asked the Buddha how to help her. The answer, in the story, was offerings to the monks, the merit dedicated to her.
Tradition links that story to festivals still kept: Ullambana in China, Obon in Japan, with lanterns, dances and family graves swept clean.
Fourth, the idea under it all: merit, punya, the good of a good act, which can be shared.
Some teachers stress this side of practice and some stress meditation more, and in some families it's both: sitting in the morning, setting out tea for grandmother at night.

how: In many Buddhist homes in Asia, families keep an altar with the Buddha and memorial tablets or photos, offer food, light and incense, and give to monks in the name of the dead, especially at festivals such as Ullambana and Obon.

o: the Buddhism of home altars, ancestor offerings and festivals
a temple run by one family, passed down from parent to child
the rule that monks must leave their families behind them

games.q: temple and family: tap the pairs.
p: the monk who helped his mother

s: the Tirokudda Sutta says weeping helps the dead
it says grief doesn't help them; giving in their name does.
the Sigalovada Sutta names offerings for departed parents as a way to honor them
the Buddha gives it to a young man as one duty toward his parents.
ancestor offerings have nothing to do with Buddhist practice
giving in the name of the dead and sharing merit are part of Buddhist life in the texts and festivals above.

games.q: you're the monk Maudgalyayana. you've seen your mother suffering after her death. what does the Buddha tell you to do?
o: use your own powers to pull her out.
make offerings to the monks and dedicate the merit to her.
games.why: in the story, his own power isn't enough. offerings to the community, made in her name, help her, and festivals like Ullambana and Obon grew from it.

practice: Let one person in your family line who has died come to mind, a grandparent, a parent, someone you know only from stories, and say their name quietly, once.
Remember one thing they gave you, a recipe, a habit, a way of laughing, and if a candle or tea is nearby, set it out for them; then sit with them a while.
If grief is heavy for you today, you don't have to carry it alone: call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Temple and family. The Buddhism of household altars, ancestor offerings and temple festivals, where giving in the name of the dead is part of practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit punya (Pali puñña): merit, the good of a good act, which Buddhists may dedicate to others, including the dead.

carryVoice: Your line: the family altar. Where the teaching and the family meet. That's today, done.

sources.ref: the Ullambana Sutra (Maudgalyayana and his mother)
